description:
Why does money grow faster the longer you leave it alone? A short, chart-driven look at compound interest: the math, the history, and the one rule that matters most.

Key points: growth on growth, the Rule of 72, and why time beats timing.
title: Compound Interest: Why Time Beats Timing

scenes.narration: Put one hundred dollars away, never add another cent, and in fifty years it has grown more than elevenfold. No luck involved. Just math.
scenes.heading: Compound Interest
scenes.text: The quiet force behind long-term wealth

scenes.narration: At five percent a year, one hundred dollars becomes about one thousand one hundred and forty seven dollars after fifty years.
scenes.heading: $100 at 5% for 50 years

scenes.narration: The trick is that each year's interest earns interest of its own. Growth stacks on top of growth.
scenes.text: Each year's interest earns interest of its own

scenes.narration: Watch a thousand dollars at five percent. Ten years: sixteen hundred. Twenty: twenty six hundred. Thirty: forty three hundred. Forty: over seven thousand.
scenes.heading: $1,000 at 5% per year

scenes.narration: People have understood this for a very long time. Babylonian clay tablets already posed compound interest problems. Richard Witt published interest tables in 1613, and Jacob Bernoulli uncovered the number e in 1683 by studying continuous compounding.
scenes.heading: A very old idea

scenes.narration: A quick shortcut: divide seventy two by the interest rate to estimate how many years it takes to double. At eight percent, that is about nine years.
scenes.heading: Rule of 72 at 8%

scenes.narration: Starting early versus starting late is not a small difference. The early saver gets extra doubling periods that the late saver can never buy back.
scenes.heading: Early vs late

scenes.narration: So the rules are simple. Start early. Reinvest what you earn. And do not interrupt it.
scenes.heading: Three rules

scenes.narration: As Charlie Munger put it: the first rule of compounding is to never interrupt it unnecessarily. Subscribe for more ideas that quietly shape your money.
scenes.text: The first rule of compounding is to never interrupt it unnecessarily.
scenes.author: Charlie Munger
